candidate.answerReason: The expression lies strictly between 969 and 970, so 970 is the smallest integer larger than it.

methods.label: Pair the expression with its conjugate
methods.explanation:
Pairing the expression with \(\sqrt3-\sqrt2\) makes it possible to obtain an exact integer sum. Set
\[
a=\sqrt3+\sqrt2,
\qquad b=\sqrt3-\sqrt2.
\]
The difference of squares and the square formulas give
\[
ab=3-2=1,
\qquad a^2+b^2=10.
\]
Multiplying out verifies the identity
\[
u^3+v^3=(u+v)\bigl((u+v)^2-3uv\bigr).
\]
Applying it with \(u=a^2\) and \(v=b^2\), whose product is \(1\), yields
\[
a^6+b^6=10(10^2-3)=970.
\]
Also \(a>1\), and \(b=1/a\), so \(0<b<1\). Hence \(0<b^6<1\), and therefore
\[
969<970-b^6=a^6<970.
\]
The smallest integer larger than \((\sqrt3+\sqrt2)^6\) is \(\boxed{970}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
methods.levelReason: Uses conjugate radicals, elementary multiplication identities and an exact interval bound.

methods.label: Expand and compare exact squares
methods.explanation:
First expand the power so that only one radical remains:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\sqrt3+\sqrt2)^6
&=(5+2\sqrt6)^3\\
&=125+150\sqrt6+360+48\sqrt6\\
&=485+198\sqrt6.
\end{aligned}
\]
To locate this number between consecutive integers, compare \(198\sqrt6\) with \(484\) and \(485\). Their squares satisfy
\[
484^2<6\cdot198^2<485^2,
\]
because the three values are respectively \(234256\), \(235224\) and \(235225\). All quantities being compared are positive, so taking square roots preserves the inequalities:
\[
484<198\sqrt6<485.
\]
Adding \(485\) gives
\[
969<(\sqrt3+\sqrt2)^6<970.
\]
Thus the requested integer is \(\boxed{970}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
methods.levelReason: Uses direct radical expansion and exact comparisons of positive squares, with no approximation.

candidate.annotationRationale: The route-neutral target is selecting the least integer strictly above a real expression by proving its exact location between integers. Radical arithmetic, square expansion and inequality manipulation support both routes. The first method uses conjugate cancellation and a sum-of-cubes identity; the second instead establishes radical bounds through exact square comparisons. The strict inequalities resolve the integer-endpoint issue.
